title: Upekkha
hookLine: equanimity: balance that doesn't abandon anyone

lines: A NURSE AT THREE IN THE MORNING.
cards: A hospice nurse sits with a frightened family at three in the morning. She's warm, but she doesn't fall apart. Dying people, angry people, grieving people, night after night, and she stays steady.
She can't fix everything, she knows it, and she keeps showing up anyway. That steadiness isn't coldness. It may be what lets her keep caring year after year.
The fourth room is built of that.

teach.h: TO LOOK UPON, FROM A BALANCED PLACE.
teach.b: Upekkha is usually translated equanimity. Pali dictionaries trace the word to a verb meaning to look upon, to look at something from a balanced place.
Picture someone standing on a hill, seeing the whole valley at once, not pulled toward one house or away from another. The Visuddhimagga's map says upekkha's mark is balance toward beings.
Its job is to see beings as equal. It shows up as the quieting of both attraction and aversion.

And its ground is a deep teaching: beings are the owners of their actions. You can love someone completely, and still not be able to live their life for them. The manual has a picture for how the four rooms fit together.
A mother has four sons. One is a baby: she wants him to grow, and that's kindness. One is sick: she wants him to get well, and that's compassion.

One is young and thriving: she wants his happiness to last, and that's gladness. And one is grown, busy with his own life: she doesn't worry over him, and that's equanimity. She hasn't stopped loving him.
She trusts him to live his own life.

teach.h: IT GROWS FROM THE OTHER THREE.
teach.b: That's why upekkha comes fourth: the manual teaches it after the other three, resting on them.

Equanimity without kindness would just be distance. With kindness underneath, it's the steadiness that lets you stay present when you can't fix things: an illness, a grown child's choice, a friend's hard road.
Tomorrow, the look-alike that tries to take its place.

how: Buddhists often practice upekkha after the other three divine abodes, often with the reflection that beings are the owners of their actions; some teachers describe it as the steadiness that keeps caregivers and practitioners present without burning out.

o: letting go of all your wishes and plans
a balance that stays warm and keeps caring
calm that comes from not getting involved

games.q: match each son in the manual's picture to a room.

s: it's balance with kindness underneath: the mother still loves her grown son.
the manual teaches upekkha after the other three
it rests on them, which is why it comes fourth.
upekkha's ground is seeing that beings own their actions
you can love someone and still not live their life for them.

games.q: your grown child makes a life choice you wouldn't have made. it's theirs to make. what does upekkha look like?
o: cut off contact until they change their mind.
stay close and caring, and trust them with their own life.
stop caring what happens to them.
games.why: in the manual's picture, the mother doesn't worry over her grown son, but she hasn't stopped loving him: balanced, not cold.

practice: Bring to mind one situation you care about but can't fix, someone's illness, someone's choice, a loss, and let yourself feel the care fully.

Then let the wish to fix it loosen a little, with the old reflection: this is their life, their path, and I can't live it for them; I can stay. Rest there, warm and steady, like the hill over the valley.

wordCard.voice: Upekkha. Equanimity: a balanced, looking-on mind that sees beings as owners of their actions and doesn't abandon anyone.

orig.note: Pali upekkhā (Sanskrit upekṣā): equanimity, from a verb meaning to look upon.

carryVoice: Your line: balanced, not cold. Warm and steady at once, even when you can't fix things. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (upekkha: characteristic, function, proximate cause; the simile of the mother with four sons)
